t: Introduction: aim and outline of the session
n: In this session we will consider labour legislation. Labour legislation regulates the relations between employee and employer. It determines questions of pay, internal rules, discipline and labour protection. Under the Labour Code, medical workers belong to the category whose working time does not exceed 36 hours a week. The reason is that their work involves high emotional and nervous strain. If sanitary rules or rules for combating epidemics are violated, a medical worker too may be the subject of an administrative offence. The outline is as follows: the employment contract, working time, labour protection, termination of the contract and disciplinary sanction. Then we move on to administrative liability.

t: Labour legislation: the Constitution and the Labour Code
n: Let us consider the main sources of labour legislation. Under Article 37 of the Constitution, every citizen has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to fair conditions of work and to protection against unemployment. The main source for regulating labour relations in line with the principles of a market economy is the Labour Code. Labour law regulates relations based on the employment contract. This includes the conclusion, amendment and termination of the contract, pay, discipline and the hearing of disputes. That is, labour law covers the whole process from the contract to its termination.

t: Labour legislation: the Constitution and the Labour Code (continued)
n: We continue. Forced labour, that is compelling someone to work under threat of punishment, is prohibited. There are also exceptions to this rule: cases such as military service, a state of emergency and a court sentence are given in Article 7 of the Labour Code. Remember: the prohibition is the general rule, and the exceptions are precisely listed in the law.

t: Distinctive features of labour relations
n: Labour relations differ from branches such as civil law by their distinctive features. Because labour is paid, it differs from activity based on public order. Remember: there are four features, designated by the letters A, B, C and D. A, production: the relation arises in production. B, member of a collective: specific rights and obligations arise. C, pay: needs are met by it. D, personal labour: the work is performed in a particular profession and post.

t: Rights of the employee and the employer
n: Now the rights of the parties. The employee has the right to receive pay not lower than the statutory minimum monthly wage, to rest, and to work in safe conditions that meet hygiene requirements. In addition, the employee has the right to vocational training and professional development, to compensation for work-related harm, and to membership of trade unions. In old age or on loss of working capacity, social security is received. Labour rights can be protected through the court and legal assistance obtained; this is given in Article 16 of the Labour Code. The employer has the right to conclude and terminate contracts and to require the employee to perform the work under the contract in full. This is stated in Article 17 of the Labour Code.

t: Obligations of the employee and the employer
n: Now the obligations. The employee must carry out the employer's lawful orders on time and accurately. The employer, in turn, cannot require work that is not within the duties, that is contrary to law, or that is dangerous to life and health. Nor is he entitled to require actions that demean the employee's honour and dignity. The employee's obligations are given in Article 176 of the Labour Code: honest and conscientious performance, observance of labour discipline, observance of safety requirements and care of the employer's property. The employer's obligations are in Article 177: organising the employees' work, ensuring discipline, observing protection rules and creating the conditions set out in the contract.

t: Quick question 1: rights and obligations
n: These are quick questions. First question: what is compelling someone to work under threat of punishment called, and does the law permit it? Second question: name at least three labour rights of an employee. Third question: which work can the employer not require of an employee? Attention: certain work performed in a state of emergency or when a court sentence has come into force is not considered forced labour. Think about the answers.

t: Employment contract: essence and content
n: We turn to the employment contract. On taking someone into employment, an employment contract is concluded. It is an agreement between employee and employer to perform work for pay. The contract must state the place of work, the job function, the time work begins, the term and the amount of pay. The stages of conclusion are as follows: first, a competition or election, if there is one; second, the employee and employer agree; third, the employment contract is concluded; fourth, the conditions of work are set, that is, place, function and start time; fifth, the term and amount of pay. The level of labour rights and guarantees established by law cannot be lowered by a contract.

t: Terms of the contract and documents on hiring
n: On the terms of the contract. The contract is concluded for an indefinite period, for a period not exceeding five years, or for the time of performing a particular job. If no term is stated, the contract is regarded as indefinite; without the employee's consent it cannot be re-drawn as fixed-term. Those entering on a part-time basis provide, instead of a work record book, a certificate from the main place of work. Documents on hiring: a passport or a document replacing it; a work record book, except for those entering for the first time; a military ID or registration certificate; and a diploma or document of specialised education.

t: Procedure of the preliminary probationary period
n: Procedure of the preliminary probationary period. The probation is carried out to test the employee's ability to work and to establish whether it is advisable to continue the employment. The probation is not more than three months; it is not set for pregnant women and women with children under three. Before the probation ends, either party may terminate the contract by giving 3 days' written notice. The process is as follows: first the probation is set, with a term of at most 3 months; to terminate, written notice is given 3 days in advance. Otherwise the contract continues.

t: The collective agreement and its principles
n: A collective agreement is a normative document regulating relations between the employer and the employees. Its principles: observance of law, competence, voluntariness, regular checking and the inevitability of liability. The draft first goes through discussion by the employees, then through the general meeting. The parties are the trade union and the employer. The content covers labour, social, economic and professional matters. As benefits there may be additional leave and a supplement to the pension. The term is set by the parties, and it remains in force until a new one is made.

t: Part-time work, combining professions and substitution
n: Let us distinguish the concepts of part-time work, combining professions and substitution. Part-time work is paid work under a contract in time free from the main job. Internal part-time work is performed in the same institution, and external part-time work in another institution. In combining professions, one works in a different post in the same institution. In substitution the work of a temporarily absent employee is performed, and that employee's post is kept. Example: the head of an institution may work in the post of doctor, and a doctor may work in the duties of a mid-level medical worker. Attention: part-time work is not substitution. In one, the work is done in free time; in the other, in place of an absent employee.

t: Case analysis 1: hiring and additional work
n: First case analysis. Situation: a doctor is being hired by a medical institution and wants also to work in another institution in his free time. For the main job a passport, work record book, military registration document and diploma are submitted; the contract states the place of work, post, start time and pay. The work in the other institution is external part-time work: instead of the work record book, a certificate from the main place of work is provided. The preliminary probation does not exceed three months. Question: which forms and documents are required? If the doctor is a woman with a child under three years, is a probation set? Answer for yourself.

t: Working time and shortened working time
n: On working time. The normal duration is 40 hours a week; the daily duration depends on the type of week. On a 6-day week it is 7 hours a day, and on a 5-day week 8 hours a day. The categories for whom shortened working time is set: persons under 18, disabled persons of groups I–II, those working in unfavourable conditions, and women with children under 3. For medical workers, working time does not exceed 36 hours a week, as given in Article 118 of the Labour Code.

t: Labour protection: duties of the parties
n: In labour protection the parties have duties. Conditions that meet safety and hygiene requirements are organised by the employer. He answers for this before the law. The employer informs the employee about working conditions, the risk of occupational disease, benefits and supplementary payments, and protective equipment. The employee, in turn, observes labour protection requirements and instructions on safe working and uses personal protective equipment. In addition, the employee promptly reports situations threatening people's life and health and work-related accidents.

t: Preliminary and periodic medical examinations
n: Preliminary and periodic medical examinations. Disabled persons, those under 18 and the elderly, those on night work and those serving the public undergo examination. The process is as follows: a preliminary examination at hiring, and a periodic examination during employment. Refusal, or failure to follow the doctor's recommendation, is grounds for removing the employee from work. An extraordinary examination can be demanded by the employee. Remember: the cost of the examination is not paid by the employee.

t: Quick question 2: working time and protection
n: The second quick question. First question: how many hours a week must the working time of medical workers not exceed? Answer: 36 hours. The work of such employees involves high emotional and mental strain and nervous stress. The list is determined by the Government. Second question: who pays for the medical examination? Answer: the employee does not pay; these costs are not laid upon him. Attention: there is a risk of error. The general norm is 40 hours a week, and for medical workers it is 36 hours.

t: Case analysis 2: refusal of a medical examination
n: Second case analysis. Situation: an employee refused a periodic medical examination or did not follow the doctor's recommendations. Question: on what legal basis does the employer act? Is the employee entitled to refuse the examination? Answer: the employee is not entitled to refuse the examination. Refusal, or failure to follow the recommendation, is grounds for removal from work. If the employee links the deterioration of his health with working conditions, he may demand an extraordinary examination.

t: Termination at the employee's initiative
n: Termination at the employee's initiative. General grounds: agreement, the initiative of one party, expiry of the term, and a circumstance independent of the parties. The employee can terminate a fixed-term or indefinite contract by giving two weeks' written notice. The procedure is as follows: first, written notice 2 weeks ahead; second, the application may be withdrawn; third, when the term expires the work ceases; fourth, the work record book is issued; fifth, the final settlement is made. If the notice period has expired and the contract has not been terminated, the application loses force.

t: Grounds for termination at the employer's initiative
n: Now the grounds for termination at the employer's initiative. Reduction of staff or volume of work, a change in technology and work organisation, or liquidation of the enterprise is the first ground. The contract may also be terminated with an employee who is insufficiently qualified or has become unfit for the work because of health. Systematic violation: a repeated offence within one year of the day a sanction was applied. A single gross violation is also grounds; gross misconduct is assessed by its consequences. Additional grounds: with part-timers because an employee who is not a part-timer is hired, and with the head of the enterprise because of a change of owner.

t: Employer's initiative: notice periods
n: Notice periods in termination at the employer's initiative. Notice is written, the employee signs; the period differs depending on the reason for termination. For staff reduction and liquidation, at least 2 months in advance, in writing, against signature. For reasons of qualification and health, at least 2 weeks in advance, in writing, against signature. For systematic or gross violation, notice is given 3 days ahead, or proportionate compensation is paid. If the parties agree, in the first two cases the notice is replaced by paid compensation corresponding to the notice period. Remember: termination is not possible during illness and leave; complete liquidation of the enterprise is an exception.

t: Case analysis 3: staff reduction and dismissal
n: Third case analysis. Situation: in a hospital, staff are being cut because the volume of work has fallen. Doctor X is at this time temporarily incapacitated, that is, ill. Question: can the employer terminate the employment contract with X precisely during the illness? The direction: termination during illness and leave is prohibited; the only exception is complete liquidation of the enterprise. A healthy employee is given written notice, against signature, of at least two months for staff reduction, or the corresponding compensation is paid.

t: Types of disciplinary sanctions
n: Types of disciplinary sanctions. Violation of labour discipline is a disciplinary offence; the employer is entitled to punish the employee. The law has three types of sanction: reprimand, fine and termination of the employment contract. Reprimand is provided for by law. A fine is up to 30 per cent of the monthly wage, and for certain offences up to 50 per cent. Termination of the contract is applied as a type of sanction. Attention: the general fine is up to 30 per cent; under the internal rules, for certain offences it may be up to 50 per cent.

t: Procedure for applying a disciplinary sanction
n: Procedure for applying a disciplinary sanction. The sanction is applied within 1 month of the offence being discovered; the employee's time on sick leave and annual leave is not included in this period. After 6 months from the offence, or 2 years if it was found in an audit, the sanction cannot be applied. The procedure is as follows: the offence is discovered, a written explanation is required, one sanction is given for one offence, the sanction is announced by order, and the sanction remains in force for 1 year. Refusal to give a written explanation is no obstacle to the sanction; the sanction can be lifted ahead of time.

t: Quick question 3: termination and disciplinary sanction
n: The third quick question. First question: if an employee wants to terminate the contract at his own initiative, how long in advance does he warn the employer? Second question: within what period after the offence is discovered may a disciplinary sanction be applied? Answer: the first, by written notice two weeks ahead; the second, within one month, not counting time on sick leave and leave. Attention: at the employee's initiative the notice is 2 weeks; if the employer terminates because of staff reduction, at least 2 months in advance.

t: Case analysis 4: disciplinary sanction
n: Fourth case analysis. Situation: a medical worker violated labour discipline and refused to give an explanation. Question: can a sanction be applied, and in what manner? A disciplinary sanction is applied within one month of the offence being discovered. The time the employee spends on sick leave or annual leave is not included in this period. Before the sanction, a written explanation is required of the employee. Refusal to give one is no obstacle to applying the sanction. For each violation only one disciplinary sanction is applied. The employee's being held to account is announced by order.

t: Administrative legislation and the concept of an offence
n: Now we turn to administrative legislation. Legislation consolidates citizens' rights and sets the procedure for liability and punishment for violations. An administrative offence is a culpable, unlawful act or omission; it is not dangerous to society. In both cases an unlawful, culpable act is the common feature. An administrative offence does not contain the feature of social danger, and administrative liability arises from it, for example violation of sanitary rules. In a crime there are features of social danger and criminal liability arises. If the significance, consequences are grave or the instances are many, the act may be assessed as a crime.

t: Forms of fault, extreme necessity and age of liability
n: Forms of fault and age of liability. Intent: foresaw the consequence, wanted it or consciously allowed it. Negligence: frivolously expected to prevent it, or should have foreseen it. If the danger cannot be eliminated otherwise, and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, the act is not an administrative offence. A person who has not reached 16 at the time of the offence is not held liable. In a minor case the body may confine itself to a warning. Attention: an administrative offence is not a crime. In the former there is no feature of social danger, and criminal liability does not arise.

t: Types of administrative penalties
n: Types of administrative penalties. Article 23 of the Code of Administrative Liability, that is the CAL, lists five types of penalty: fine, paid seizure, confiscation, deprivation of a special right and administrative arrest. A principal penalty, or a principal and an additional one, is imposed; seizure and confiscation can be both. For professional offences of medical workers, a fine is imposed in most cases.

t: Amount of the fine: citizen and official
n: Amount of the fine. The fine is calculated from the minimum monthly wage; the amount at the time the offence was committed is taken. For a continuing offence, the minimum wage at the time the offence was discovered is the basis. A fine is a monetary penalty paid to the state; the amount differs for a citizen and an official. For a citizen the smallest is not less than 1/50, the largest not more than 5 times, in exceptional cases up to 100 times, and by local decision up to 3 times. For an official the smallest is not less than 1/10, the largest not more than 10 times, in exceptional cases up to 150 times, and by local decision up to 5 times.

t: Time limits for applying an administrative penalty
n: Time limits for applying an administrative penalty. The penalty is applied within 2 months of the day the offence was committed, or if it is continuing, of the day of discovery. If initiation of a criminal case is refused or the case is closed, it is applied within 1 month of the day of the decision. The decision on confiscation is issued by the judge for administrative cases of the district or city court, and by the tax and customs authorities.

t: Quick question 4: foundations of administrative liability
n: The fourth quick question. First question: from what age does administrative liability begin? Answer: a person who has not reached 16 at the time of the offence is not held liable. Second question: which penalty is applied more often for professional offences of medical workers? Answer: in most cases a fine. If the offence is minor, the body hearing the case may release from liability and confine itself to a warning. Attention: an administrative offence is not a crime. But if the consequences are grave, some offences may be assessed as crimes.

t: Bodies hearing the case, and expert examination
n: Bodies hearing the case. Cases are heard by the judge for administrative cases of the district or city court and by economic courts. They are also heard by administrative commissions attached to self-governing bodies and commissions for juvenile affairs. They are also heard by internal affairs bodies and state inspectorates. Among them are the State Sanitary Supervision and labour inspectors. If special knowledge is needed, the body handling the case orders an expert examination. Its rules are the same as in criminal and civil cases.

t: Drawing up the record and the person's rights
n: Drawing up the record and the person's rights. The record states the date, place, essence of the offence, the regulatory act and the explanation. The procedure: the record is drawn up, the person's rights are explained, and the person who drew up the record, the offender and a witness sign. If a signature is not given, a note is made. There is also the right to lodge a complaint. The person studies the case and uses an advocate and an interpreter; this is given in Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Liability. The injured party, that is the victim, has the same rights in the case as the accused.

t: Administrative offences of medical workers
n: Administrative offences of medical workers. Chapter VI of the Code contains acts in the sphere of health; the subject may be a medical worker as well. Articles such as slander and insult relate more to the heads of medical institutions. Officials are answerable for violating the procedure for submitting state statistical reports. Groups of offences: health sphere, Articles 52–56, sanitation, epidemics, narcotics. Venereal disease and AIDS, Articles 57–59, concealing the source, refusing examination. Trade and finance, Articles 164, 176, 176-1, paid services, entrepreneurship, contract. Order of administration, Articles 199 and 215, false call to emergency services and reporting.

t: Offences concerning sexually transmitted diseases, AIDS and the order of administration
n: Offences concerning sexually transmitted diseases, AIDS and the order of administration. Article 57: if a patient with a sexually transmitted disease or AIDS conceals the source of infection or persons whose contact creates a danger, it is an administrative offence. Article 58: refusing examination despite sufficient information about the disease may also entail administrative liability. Article 59: if safety is not ensured in examination to detect AIDS infection, or in medical and cosmetic procedures, medical workers are answerable. Article 199: knowingly false call to emergency services, the subject being a citizen. Article 215: violation of the procedure for statistical reporting, the subject being an official.

t: Case analysis 5: violation of sanitary rules
n: Fifth case analysis. Situation: a sanitary or anti-epidemic rule was violated in an institution; an authorised official drew up a record. The record states the date, place, essence of the act, the regulatory act, witnesses and the explanation; both sides sign it. Under Article 294 the person's rights are explained: familiarisation with the case, advocate, native language, interpreter and appeal. Question: who is liable, and what penalty? A medical worker too may be the subject; usually a fine, applied within two months of the act.

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Conclusion and review questions. An employee terminates the contract by giving two weeks' written notice. A disciplinary sanction is applied within one month, and one for one offence. The working time of medical workers does not exceed 36 hours a week. The employer carries out preliminary and periodic medical examinations. Attention: an administrative offence is not a crime, since it lacks the feature of social danger. Liability begins from 16; a fine is most often applied to a medical worker. For the final discussion, answer the review questions on rights, the contract, termination, types of sanction and the requirements for the record.
